```{r libs}
library(ctsem)
library(ggplot2)
```

`intoverpop = 'laplace'` integrates individual differences in parameters out
of the likelihood with a Laplace approximation. The `id` argument can be a
*vector* of id columns, so subjects can be nested in studies, sites or
classrooms, with random effects at each level.

This vignette describes the approximation, how to specify and fit such a
model, and how to read, plot and extract the results. It requires the Julia
backend.

# The model

## Where random effects live

ctsem works internally with a vector of raw, unconstrained parameters
$\theta$, and each model matrix cell is a function of one raw value through
that parameter's transform. When parameters vary across individuals, each
subject $i$ has its own raw vector:

$$
v_i \;=\; \theta \;+\; \sum_{l} L_l\, u_{b_l(i)}, \qquad u \sim N(0, I)
$$

Here $l$ indexes the levels of the hierarchy, $b_l(i)$ is the group that
subject $i$ belongs to at level $l$ (itself at the subject level, its study at
the study level), and $L_l$ is the Cholesky factor of that level's population
covariance, built from raw standard-deviation and correlation parameters. The
shifts are additive on the raw scale and are applied before the transforms, so
a subject's parameter and the population parameter are always on the same
scale.

Because $u$ is standard normal, the spread of individual differences is
described by $L_l$, which is what `popsd` and `rawpopcorr` report.

## Two ways to integrate over $u$

The likelihood needed is the marginal one, with $u$ integrated out. ctsem has
two ways to do this.

**Augmentation** (`intoverpop = 'augmented'`) adds $u$ to the latent state with
no drift and no diffusion, so the Kalman filter integrates over it as part of
filtering. This is exact for random effects that shift a mean in a linear
Gaussian model, and a linearisation otherwise. Every subject's filtered system
grows from $n$ latent processes to $n + k$, where $k$ is the number of varying
parameters, and the cost of the filter is cubic in that dimension.

**Laplace** (`intoverpop = 'laplace'`) keeps every subject's system at $n$
latent processes and approximates the integral. For a group of members $U$
that share a random effect,

$$
T(\theta) \;=\; \log \int \exp\Big( \textstyle\sum_{m \in U} \ell_m(v_m) - \tfrac{1}{2}u'u \Big)\, du
\;-\; \tfrac{d}{2}\log 2\pi
$$

is approximated by expanding the exponent about its mode $\hat u$:

$$
T(\theta) \;\approx\; \sum_{m \in U} \ell_m\big(v_m(\theta, \hat u)\big) \;-\; \tfrac{1}{2}\hat u'\hat u \;-\; \tfrac{1}{2}\log\det M,
\qquad M = I - A
$$

where $A$ is the Hessian of $\sum_m \ell_m$ with respect to $u$ at the mode,
and the identity in $M$ is the curvature of the standard normal prior.

The mode is found by Newton's method within each evaluation, and the gradient
with respect to $\theta$ is exact, so the only approximation is in the
integral itself.

## When the approximation is exact

When a random effect enters the state mean linearly, through an identity
transform, in a linear Gaussian model, the integrand is exactly Gaussian in
$u$ and the Laplace approximation gives the exact integral. `T0MEANS`, `CINT`
and `MANIFESTMEANS` have identity transforms by default, so the model below is
of this kind.

The approximation is not exact when the effect enters through a nonlinear
transform (`DRIFT`, `DIFFUSION`, and any state dependent parameter). It is
better the more each subject's data say about that subject's own effects.

By default `ctFit()` checks the size of that error (the random-effects
check, `optimcontrol$checks`). It evaluates the integral for each subject, or
for each outermost group when levels are nested, at draws from its posterior,
and says so if computing the integrals exactly would move an estimate by a
tenth of a standard error or more, with a warning from one standard error. `ctFitUncertainty(fit, intoverpop = 'quadrature')`
then refines the fit, integrating the flagged units by quadrature and
reporting the quadrature log likelihood, and `ctFit(intoverpop = 'quadrature')`
does the same when fitting. `print(fit)` says when the estimate moved, or
should have.

`ctLaplaceCheck()` reports the same check for any Laplace fit, as how far the
estimate would move if the integral were computed exactly. Values of
`delta_se` well below one mean the approximation does not limit the result,
and values near or above one mean it does. Read `dropped_directions` as well.
A direction the data do not identify well enough to correct along is also
reported as a zero correction in `delta_se`, which then means the correction
could not be estimated. `ctFitUncertainty(fit, 'is', intoverpop =
'quadrature')` importance samples against the quadrature posterior, which
corrects the shape of the intervals as well as their centre.

The refined fit has its own estimate and curvature, but its intervals are
still a normal approximation at a mode, which understates the skew of a
population standard deviation estimated from few groups.
`ctFitUncertainty(fit, 'sample', intoverpop = 'none')` samples the parameters
and every unit's random effects jointly, which avoids the approximation. On a
fit made with `intoverpop = 'laplace'`, as here, `ctFitUncertainty(fit,
'sample')` without `intoverpop` samples the Laplace approximation of the
marginal likelihood instead, and keeps its error. A short run is often enough
to improve on the normal approximation (`vignette('uncertainty')`).

## Nesting

Subjects in the same study share that study's random effect, so their
likelihood contributions cannot be integrated separately. The unit of
integration is therefore the **outermost group**, here a study with all of its
subjects.

For a study of 100 subjects with 2 subject effects and 1 study effect, that
integral is 201-dimensional. It is still cheap, because each subject's block of
the curvature is linked only to its study's block (an *arrow* structure), and
ctsem factorises it block by block. The cost therefore grows linearly with the
number of subjects.

# A worked example

## Simulating

Thirty subjects in five studies, with ten occasions each. The process is a
univariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process in which subjects differ in their
starting level (`T0MEANS`) and their equilibrium (`CINT`), with a correlation
of $-0.4$ between the two, and studies also differ in their average
equilibrium.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(4)
nstudy <- 5; npersub <- 6; nobs <- 10
mu_cint <- 0.3; drift <- -0.4; diffusion <- 0.6; merror <- 0.2
sd_study_cint <- 0.5
sd_sub_cint <- 0.4; sd_sub_t0 <- 0.8; rho <- -0.4

gm <- ctModel(type = 'ct', id = c('id', 'study'),
  manifestNames = 'Y1', latentNames = 'eta1', LAMBDA = matrix(1),
  T0MEANS = matrix('t0||id'), CINT = matrix('cint||TRUE'), DRIFT = matrix(drift),
  DIFFUSION = matrix(diffusion), MANIFESTVAR = matrix(merror),
  MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(0), T0VAR = matrix(0))

# The population covariances, on the raw scale: T0MEANS and CINT are 10 times
# their raw parameter, so a covariance is a hundredth of its natural value and
# an sd a tenth.
S <- matrix(c(sd_sub_t0^2, rho * sd_sub_t0 * sd_sub_cint,
              rho * sd_sub_t0 * sd_sub_cint, sd_sub_cint^2), 2, 2,
  dimnames = list(c('t0', 'cint'), c('t0', 'cint')))
gm$RAWPOPVAR <- ctCov(S / 100)
gm$RAWPOPVAR_study['cint', 'cint'] <- sd_study_cint / 10

dat <- ctGenerate(gm, n = c(nstudy * npersub, nstudy), Tpoints = nobs,
  backend = 'julia', values = c(t0 = 0, cint = mu_cint))
# What each subject and each study was generated with.
truth <- attr(dat, 'subjectpars')
studytruth <- attr(dat, 'grouppars')$study
dat <- data.frame(dat)
head(dat)
```

`study` is an ordinary column of the long data frame, constant within each
subject. ctsem reads the nesting from the data.

## Specifying the hierarchy

Give `id` a vector of column names, innermost first:

```{r model}
m <- ctModel(type = 'ct', id = c('id', 'study'),
  manifestNames = 'Y1', latentNames = 'eta1', LAMBDA = matrix(1),
  T0MEANS = matrix('T0m_eta1||id'), CINT = matrix('cint_eta1'),
  MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(0))
```

By default ctsem fixes `CINT` to zero and estimates the level in
`MANIFESTMEANS`. Here `CINT` is free and `MANIFESTMEANS` fixed instead, so that
the process has an equilibrium at $-\text{CINT}/\text{DRIFT}$ for individual
differences to act on.

A cell's `indvarying` field says at which levels its parameter varies: `TRUE`
for every level, `FALSE` for none, or the names of levels. Intercepts that are
not specified vary at every level, so `cint_eta1` varies both between subjects
and between studies, and its variance splits into a within-study and a
between-study part. `'T0m_eta1||id'` lets the starting level vary between
subjects only. `'cint_eta1||study'` would let the equilibrium vary between
studies only, with the subjects in a study sharing one value. The same field
can be written by name, `'T0m_eta1, indvarying=id'`, or with
`ctPar('T0m_eta1', indvarying = 'id')`. Printing the model shows what varies
where, and what each level will estimate:

```{r levels-print}
print(m, matrices = FALSE)
```

`m$pars$indvarying` holds the same values, one per cell, and can be edited
directly, with `TRUE`, `FALSE` or level names as in a cell. A cell's `sdscale`
scales the prior on the standard deviation at every level the parameter varies
at. Levels must be **strictly nested**, with every subject in exactly one
study. ctsem checks this and stops if the data say otherwise.

## Fitting

```{r fit}
fit <- ctFit(dat, m, backend = 'julia', intoverpop = 'laplace', cores = 4)
```

`cores` sets the number of threads used for the integration units, which are
studies here. `intoverpop = 'laplace'` requires `backend = 'julia'`. With
`optimize = FALSE` the same model is sampled instead, with the random effects
drawn along with the parameters, and the Laplace approximation is not used.

# Reading the output

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

The parts specific to a hierarchy:

**`Random-effects standard deviations (id)`** and **`(study)`** are the spread
of the random effects at each level, on the transformed parameter scale. With
more than one level, each table is labelled with its level.

Together they decompose the variance. `cint_eta1` varies at both levels, so its
total variation splits into a within-study part and a between-study part,
here against generating values of $0.4$ and $0.5$:

```{r decomp}
s <- summary(fit)
rbind(
  estimated = c(id = s$popsd.id['cint_eta1', 'mean'],
                study = s$popsd.study['cint_eta1', 'mean']),
  truth = c(id = sd_sub_cint, study = sd_study_cint))
```

**`Random-effects correlations (id)`** are correlations between random effects
on the raw parameter scale. For parameters with identity transforms, like
these, they are also the correlations of the transformed parameters, but for
`DRIFT` or `DIFFUSION` they are not. The study level has only one effect here,
so it has no correlation table.

**`Fixed-effects / Population means`** are the population values, the
parameters before any random effects are added.

`summary(fit)$randomEffects` holds the same quantities for each level, as raw
draws:

```{r payload}
str(lapply(summary(fit)$randomEffects, function(z)
  list(level = z$level, popsd = colnames(z$popsd))))
```

# Per-subject parameters

`ctSubjectPars()` returns each subject's parameter values: the population
value plus its random effects at every level it belongs to, plus any time
independent predictor effects, passed through the model's transforms:

```{r subjectpars}
sp <- ctSubjectPars(fit)
dim(sp)
round(head(sp[1, , ], 4), 3)
```

The array is `draws x subjects x parameters`. A Laplace fit gives one draw,
the conditional modes at the estimated population parameters, which is a point
estimate.

Against the values that generated the data:

```{r recovery}
c(cint = cor(sp[1, , 'cint_eta1'], truth$cint),
  T0means = cor(sp[1, , 'T0m_eta1'], truth$t0))
```

Because `cint_eta1` varies at both levels, the subject estimates include the
study effects. Each study's own value, the population value plus that study's
effect, comes from `level = 'study'`:

```{r studymeans}
st <- ctSubjectPars(fit, level = 'study')
round(rbind(estimated = st[1, , 'cint_eta1'], truth = studytruth$cint), 3)
```

```{r studyplot, fig.height = 4}
d <- data.frame(cint = sp[1, , 'cint_eta1'], study = factor(truth$study))
ggplot(d, aes(x = study, y = cint, colour = study)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(d$cint), linetype = 'dashed', colour = 'grey50') +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = .12, height = 0), size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = 'crossbar', width = .5, colour = 'black') +
  labs(y = 'subject CINT', title = 'Subject equilibria, grouped by study') +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = 'none')
```

The spread of the black study means around the dashed grand mean is the
between-study variation, and the scatter within each study is the
within-study variation.

# Trajectories

`ctPredict()` and `ctKalman()` work as for any other fit:

```{r predict}
k <- ctPredict(fit, subjects = c(1, 7, 13), timestep = .25,
  timerange = c(0, 9))
plot(k)
```

## Choosing which levels enter the trajectory

`randomEffects` selects the levels whose random effects the trajectory uses.
Naming an id column includes that level and every level *above* it:

- `'id'` (the default, the innermost id) gives each subject its own trajectory;
- `'study'` gives the study mean, shared by every subject in a study;
- `'population'` includes no random effects, giving the trajectory implied by
  the population parameters alone.

The difference is clearest in the expectation at each subject's first
observation, which comes from the parameters before any observation updates
it:

```{r levels}
subs <- c(1, 7, 13, 19, 25)   # one from each study
sapply(c('id', 'study', 'population'), function(lev) {
  p <- ctPredict(fit, subjects = subs, timestep = .5, timerange = c(0, 9),
    randomEffects = lev)
  round(p$value[p$Element %in% 'yprior' & p$Time == 0], 3)
})
```

Under `'id'` each subject starts at its own estimated `T0MEANS`. Under
`'study'` and `'population'` they all start at the same value, because
`T0MEANS` varies only between subjects here. The study effect is on `CINT`, so
it changes where the trajectories go, and not where they begin.

## Which data the trajectories use

On a Laplace fit with one level of random effects, the predicted and updated
trajectories use random effects estimated from each subject's earlier data
only, as a filter would, and smoothed trajectories use the whole record. With
nested levels, as here, the random effects are estimated from each subject's
whole record, so even `yprior` depends on the complete series. These are
smoothed trajectories, and predictions from them are not out-of-sample
forecasts. ctsem prints a message saying which applies.

On this fit the random effects are not estimated again for a prediction. They
are the ones the fit found, from the data the fit used, and stay fixed when a
prediction call changes the rows being filtered, by selecting subjects,
interpolating onto a time grid, or withholding observations with `removeObs`.
A prediction with every observation withheld still uses that subject's own
random effects, and so is a prediction for that subject:

```{r fixedmodes}
firstrow <- function(...) {
  k <- ctPredict(fit, subjects = c(1, 7, 13), ...)
  v <- k[k$Element %in% 'yprior', ]
  v <- v[order(v$Subject, v$Time), ]
  round(unlist(lapply(split(v, v$Subject), function(d) d$value[1])), 3)
}
rbind(
  `as observed` = firstrow(timestep = 'asdata'),
  interpolated  = firstrow(timestep = .5, timerange = c(0, 9)),
  `no data`     = firstrow(timestep = .5, timerange = c(0, 9), removeObs = TRUE))
```

# Practical notes

**How many groups at the outer level.** A level's standard deviation is
estimated from the number of *groups* at that level, not the number of
subjects. Five studies is few, and the interval on `popsd.study` above is wide
accordingly. With very few groups the correlations can run to their limits.
ctsem holds them just short of $\pm 1$ and warns when a fit ends there.

**Priors** are available at every level, and help when an outer level is
weakly identified.

**Laplace or augmentation.** `intoverpop = TRUE`, and the default `'auto'`
when optimizing, use the Laplace approximation on the julia backend. Random
effects that shift a mean in a linear Gaussian model are integrated exactly
within each subject's filter, as augmentation would, and other effects by the
Laplace approximation. It is the only option for nesting above the subject
level. Augmentation can be chosen with `intoverpop = 'augmented'`, and can be
faster for a random parameter shared by several cells.

**Time independent predictors** work at any level, as long as the predictor
varies at that level.
